newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's patchwork democracy doomed to failure.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's patchwork democracy doomed to failure.

text.p: Fighting in Phnom Penh between troops loyal to Cambodia's rival prime ministers confirmed for many what they had long suspected -- the country's flawed attempt at democracy was doomed to failure.

After decades of war and violent revolution, Cambodia's brief period of relative stablity came to an explosive end when troops under Second Prime Minister Hun Sen moved against his co-premier's forces on Saturday.
"Whatever progress had been made in the last five years, and it isn't much, is gone," said one gloomy political analyst on Sunday.
The two men formed their uneasy coalition in 1993 following U.N.-supervised elections.

First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party, which until 1991 had battled Hun Sen's Hanoi-backed government from remote guerrilla bases on the border the with Thailand, won the polls.
But Hun Sen, who despite the U.N. presence in the country retained control of the administrative and security apparatus, objected to the results.
After a brief period of political chaos, King Norodom Sihanouk persuaded his son Ranariddh and Hun Sen to form their coalition.
"The biggest flaw was that the U.N. failed to complete its mission," a diplomat said.
"The international community was bullied into a power-sharing arrangement. It may have been the only tenable solution at the time but it has come back to haunt us," he said.
Fighting erupted on Saturday after Hun Sen said he was ordering his forces to take action against "illegal troops" being brought into the capital by Ranariddh.

Hun Sen, whose men outnumber those of the prince in the capital, justified his move by saying the prince was bringing defectors from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group into the city to reinforce his strength.
Ranariddh denied the charge and said later that Hum Sen was attempting a coup.
Analysts said on Sunday there was virtually no hope of the two leaders ever getting their government back together again.
"I would say that the chances of that are zero," said a diplomat. "Its impossible to come back from this one."
The seeds of Cambodia's crisis were sown during the U.N. operation in the country which began after a 1991 peace treaty and ended soon after the May 1993 elections, analysts said.
"The United Nations never neutralised the civil service and the bureaucratic apparatus," said a Cambodian scholar who declined to be identified.

The world body tried to foster reconcilation by sharing the machinery of state equally between the two men, creating posts for two premiers, dual posts in all ministries and in provincial administrations.
But instead of encouraging reconciliation, the structure exacerbated the differences that already existed, the scholar said.

"Instead of a one-party state we've got two separate one-party states, and they are fighting each other." A bitter struggle for power erupted in March last year when Ranariddh threatened to leave the coalition unless he got more power to govern in the provinces.

As that row gathered steam, Ranariddh opened peace talks with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group, hoping to win glory by ending the long running war and looking for a deal with more moderate rebel leaders to boost his chances in elections scheduled for next May.
Analysts said the possibility of a deal between Ranariddh and Khmer Rouge political leader Khieu Samphan might have been the final straw for Hun Sen.
